request.question: I teach a mixed class of fourteen-year-olds in a mountain town, and next term we are spending six weeks on high places and cold places. Last year the unit was mostly reading and a few videos, and the students said it felt like someone else's story. This year I want them to work with a real record and to argue carefully about what it shows. Some of them have relatives who herd yaks, and they hear many stories about the snow arriving later or leaving earlier, or about roads that used to close for weeks. I do not want to tell them those stories are right or wrong; I want them to look at a long record, see what it says and what it cannot say, and write down their doubts. I know that a model grid cell is large and that one cell over high mountains will not match one valley. I also know that a single line through noisy years can mislead, so I would like them to see the yearly values first and only then talk about rates. We will spend one lesson on what a reanalysis is, one on units, and one on why a short record is weak evidence. The students will work in pairs and present a short summary at the end. Please keep it simple enough for them, and do not suggest anything that needs a paid account or special software. So, concretely: please set up snow depth on the Tibetan Plateau from 1990 to 2020.

Some context, in case it matters: I am a retired harbour pilot and I am writing a short memoir chapter about the winters I worked on Cook Inlet. My notes from those years are patchy. My grandson says there is a free NASA record that might help me check my memory against something more systematic. I understand it will be a large grid cell and not the exact inlet, and that a model estimate is not the same as what I saw from the bridge. I am not looking for a forecast, and I do not need anything about the causes. I just want to see the yearly values laid out so I can compare them with my notes, and I would like to keep the period to the years I actually worked. Please do not change the dates; if the record does not cover them, tell me rather than picking other years. Thank you for your patience with an old sailor.
